# Steam and oven spring

Oven spring is the rapid expansion a loaf makes in its first minutes of baking: gases trapped in the dough expand and yeast gives a final burst of activity before dying around sixty degrees. A moist oven surface delays crust formation during those minutes, letting the loaf stretch upward instead of tearing at random spots.

A cast-iron Dutch oven is the reliable home method. Preheated with the lid on, it radiates intense bottom heat and traps the loaf's own escaping moisture as steam for the first twenty minutes; removing the lid then lets the crust brown and crisp. On an open baking stone the same effect needs added steam — a preheated metal pan below the stone receiving a cup of boiling water at loading produces a burst of vapor for the early minutes.

Scoring — deliberate slashes across the top of the loaf — directs the expansion where the baker wants it instead of letting the crust split wherever it is weakest. A shallow confident cut at an angle produces the lifted ear; timid scratches seal over. The enemies of good spring are an underproofed tight dough that bursts explosively and an overproofed slack one with no expansion left. Cold dough straight from a final proof in the refrigerator scores cleanly and springs harder than a warm slack loaf.
